clue.text: Most formal couple of streets housing King's grandson

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it inside, so the street pair wraps around the grandson

parts.note: two lots of ST, the abbreviation for street
Prince Harry's son is a grandson of King Charles III

explanation.surface: A royal youngster is squeezed between two of the stuffiest streets in town.
explanation.walkthrough: The two STs sit either side of ARCHIE to give STARCHIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Starchy describes stiff, prim behaviour, so the superlative is the stiffest or most formal.

clue.text: Get back from African country, climbing inspiring area

indicators.note: in a down entry something climbing goes upward, so its letters are read bottom to top
to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the country takes a letter inside it

parts.note: the West African state
A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Someone recovers something, perhaps territory, from an African nation while on a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: NIGER upwards is REGIN, and A goes inside it to make REGAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To regain something is to recover possession of it, a plain synonym for getting it back.

clue.text: Rock singer hosting show at intervals for composer

indicators.note: a host holds guests within, so the shaken word wraps around the chosen letters
to rock is to shake about, so the word after it is jolted into a new order

parts.note: the word as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: taking letters at intervals means skipping every other one

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of this word

explanation.surface: A rock vocalist puts on a show from time to time in honour of a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock singer' looks like a genre of performer, but Rock is the anagram signal working on singer.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gershwin was the American composer of Rhapsody in Blue and Porgy and Bess.

clue.text: Blood once obtained from Cambridge college student finally

parts.note: Clare College is one of the University of Cambridge colleges

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the preceding word, keeping only its closing letter

parts.note: the last letter of this word

explanation.surface: Blood is drawn from a Cambridge undergraduate, perhaps in a boxing bout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks the definition as dated: claret was old slang, especially in boxing, for blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret, the red Bordeaux wine, was formerly used as a slang word for blood because of its colour.

clue.text: Rower has mobile charger

indicators.note: something mobile moves about, so these letters are free to move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An oarsman carries a portable phone charger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charger' reads as an electrical gadget, but it is the old word for a cavalry horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger is a horse ridden into battle, which is exactly what a warhorse is.

clue.text: Advertise proposed law

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to announce or promote, as on a poster
second meaning: a draft statute put before parliament

explanation.surface: Someone publicises a piece of draft legislation.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to announce on a poster; as a noun it is a draft act laid before parliament.

clue.text: Something reflective of musical I heard

parts.note: Cats is Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical

indicators.note: heard tells us to take the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: the pronoun and the organ of sight are pronounced the same

explanation.surface: Someone muses on something from a stage show that they listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat's-eye is a British road stud with glass reflectors that shine in headlights.
explanation.definitionFit: Cat's-eyes are reflective studs set into road surfaces to mark lanes at night.

clue.text: Harry almost coping with a person ringing the changes?

indicators.note: to harry is to harass and disturb, so the following letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Harry is only just managing, alongside someone shaking things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' looks like a deletion signal but is simply fodder. 'Ringing the changes' is literal: change-ringing is the art of sounding church bells in sequences.
explanation.definitionFit: A campanologist is a bell-ringer, and change-ringing is the bell-ringing practice of sounding varying sequences.

clue.text: Principal resigning has change of heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter, and a change of heart swaps that letter for another

parts.note: someone resigning is leaving their post

explanation.surface: A head teacher who quits has second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle V of LEAVING becomes D, giving LEADING. 'Principal' sounds like a head teacher but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Leading and principal both mean chief or foremost, as in the leading role or principal role.

clue.text: Worldwide travellers Derek and Rodney supporting Shakespearean theatre

indicators.note: in a down entry a support sits underneath, so the brothers' surname is placed below the playhouse

parts.note: the Globe was the London playhouse of Shakespeare's company
Del Boy and Rodney Trotter, the brothers in the BBC sitcom Only Fools and Horses

explanation.surface: Two sitcom brothers back a famous Elizabethan playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'supporting' means sitting underneath, so the brothers' surname goes below the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Globetrotters are people who travel widely around the world, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Retiring Greeks regularly worry about male duck

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the whole string of letters is read from right to left
regularly asks for letters at a steady spacing, here every second one

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word
to nag is to pester or worry someone
RE means about or concerning
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: Shy Greeks habitually fret over a drake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' acts on everything that follows it, not only on Greeks.
explanation.definitionFit: The merganser is a fish-eating diving duck with a narrow serrated bill.

clue.text: Good day to get magazine

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the British celebrity weekly ...!

explanation.surface: A pleasant day out spent picking up a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity gossip magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are greetings said on meeting someone, and the same word is the title of a celebrity weekly.

clue.text: That woman wears coat from Amazon in grey

indicators.note: a person wears a coat around them, so she goes inside the outer layer
a coat is the outside layer, so only the first and last letters of the next word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
the pronoun for that woman

explanation.surface: A woman sports a grey coat bought online from Amazon.
explanation.walkthrough: SHE sits inside A...N.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen means pale or ash-coloured, a shade of grey, as in an ashen face.

clue.text: Scandal emerging from regatta we organised

indicators.note: organised means put into a fresh arrangement, so these letters are set out in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scandal breaks out at a boat race that we put on.
explanation.definitionFit: Watergate was the 1970s US political scandal that brought down President Nixon, and its name is used for any major scandal.

clue.text: Austere sailor promises to pay grasping family

indicators.note: to grasp is to hold tight, so the sailor and promises close around the family

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
a stem is a line of descent in a family tree
an IOU is a written promise to pay a debt

explanation.surface: A frugal seaman signs IOUs while clinging on to his relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: AB and IOUS together grasp STEM in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstemious means self-denying in food and drink, which is close to austere in its sense of plain and self-disciplined.

clue.text: Occupy two terms playing cricket?

parts.note: first term: a set of six balls bowled from one end
second term: a single scored by running between the wickets

explanation.surface: Someone takes up a pair of cricketing words, perhaps in a quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls from one bowler and a run is the basic unit of scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: To overrun a country is to invade and occupy it in large numbers.

clue.text: School subject, first one calling for changes

parts.note: RE is religious education, a British school subject
the former of two is the first

explanation.surface: A school timetable item: first up, someone campaigning for change.
explanation.definitionFit: A reformer campaigns for improvement or change, especially in politics or society.

clue.text: Cruel sister rude occasionally about furniture item

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the kept letters are read backwards
occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of the phrase is kept

parts.note: the even-placed letters of this phrase

explanation.surface: A wicked sister is now and then rude about a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters run across all three words, and 'about' then turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: A dresser is a sideboard with shelves above for displaying plates, a piece of kitchen furniture.

clue.text: Boxing trophy, originally worked out it's knocked off

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing in a box, so one word holds another inside

parts.note: to deduce is to work out by reasoning

indicators.note: originally points to the origin of the word, its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A boxer's trophy, initially won, is knocked off its stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' and 'knocked' paint a fight, but Boxing is the container signal: T goes inside DEDUCED.
explanation.definitionFit: Deducted means taken off a total, and to knock something off a price is to subtract it.

clue.text: Immediately like a card that's been played?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: at once, without further thought, as in rejected summarily

definitions.text: like a card that's been played?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, taken literally: no longer held among the player's cards

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading of the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at once or summarily, and a played card has literally left the player's hand.

clue.text: Excellent firm inside runs new cooling system

indicators.note: inside places the firm within the letters that follow it

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, with the digit 1 read as the letter I
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
CO is the abbreviation for company
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A first-rate company installs a new air-conditioning setup.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is a common way of saying excellent; crosswords often let the 1 stand as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Air-con is short for air-conditioning, the system that keeps a building or car cool.

clue.text: Delightful sequel broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means put out over the airwaves, so we want the spoken sound

parts.note: a suite is a train of followers, an old sense of sequel

explanation.surface: A charming follow-up is shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: Sequel here is not a follow-up film but its older sense of a retinue, which is a suite.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet means charming or pleasing, as in a sweet little cottage.

clue.text: Bourgeois figure

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a four-sided shape with equal sides and right angles

explanation.definitionFit: A square is slang for a conventional, unfashionable person and is also a geometric shape.

clue.text: Suffer at home before detailed remedy

indicators.note: de-tailed read as having its tail removed, so the last letter goes

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
a cure is a remedy

explanation.surface: Someone falls ill at home before receiving a thorough treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' looks like thorough, but split as de-tailed it trims the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a loss or penalty is to suffer it or bring it on oneself.

clue.text: My chrysanthemum essentially shows little growth

parts.note: Cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like My!

indicators.note: the essence of a word is taken as its very centre, the middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of this thirteen-letter word

explanation.surface: A gardener says their chrysanthemum has barely grown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little growth' sounds horticultural but means a small hard growth on the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A corn is a small patch of hardened skin on the foot, a little growth in the medical sense.

clue.text: Sore over source of sponsorship I have withdrawn

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word for sore is read backwards

parts.note: an ulcer is an open sore

indicators.note: the source of something is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of this word
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: Someone is upset that their sponsor has pulled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withdrawn' looks like it describes the sponsorship but is the definition, an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A recluse lives apart from society, so reclusive describes someone withdrawn and solitary.

clue.text: Poor Ted is jittery wreck

indicators.note: jittery means nervous and shaky, so the letters are jolted out of place

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Unfortunate Ted is a nervous wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wreck' reads as a noun, as in a nervous wreck, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To torpedo a plan is to wreck or ruin it, from the weapon that sinks ships.

clue.text: Reprimands appear fulsome to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only part of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Telling-offs can seem overdone in part.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting an earful means being scolded at length, so earfuls are reprimands.
